Modern research draws on cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and computer science to investigate how language is processed. The course focuses primarily, though not exclusively, on the neuroscience of language. Students examine theoretical and experimental issues in speech production and comprehension, language impairments, the relationship between thought and language, and the evolution and acquisition of language. Topics covered: What is language? analysis: The closest plan joins Psycholinguistics, neurobiology, perception and higher cognition with stylistics, rhetoric, philosophical theories of mind, empirical statistics and synthesis of research. Lifespan Developmental Psychology supplies developmental context, while child language acquisition is specifically evidenced in Psycholinguistics. The description-only perception and psycholinguistics courses supply meaningful direct or enabling content. The society option replaces peripheral archaeology and art selections with a sequence in sociology, community rhetoric, brain and behavior and Psycholinguistics. Stylistics and discourse, multilingual cognition, community speaking, qualitative research, social theory and media representation give complementary language and society perspectives. It offers qualitative field methods for social questions rather than phonological fieldwork. The computational plan combines Python, logic, probability, linear algebra and data methods with machine learning, neural language models, stylistics and psycholinguistics. Computer vision contributes transferable pattern recognition; general AI decision and optimization courses do not count as language modelling on their own. The computational option covers selected elements of language computation, with no dedicated corpus-linguistics sequence. The three options exceed the pairwise four-course threshold. Four bounded pairings cover meaning, methods, language processing and digital data. Dedicated grammar, speech sounds and fieldwork remain visible as distinct external subjects. The required Utrecht thesis and the optional 15 EC UCR comparison element are separately identified.

alignment.rationale: Both study how linguistic choices shape meaning. UCR approaches this through stylistics, dialogue and discourse.
Both examine human language processing. UCR covers experimental approaches alongside neuroscience, bilingualism and language disorders.
Utrecht introduces linguistics as a field of study.
Utrecht has a dedicated introduction to language psychology. UCR studies related processes in psycholinguistics and other cognition courses.
Utrecht compares how languages build words and sentences. UCR touches on these features in stylistics.
Utrecht studies how language develops. UCR offers broader developmental psychology and psycholinguistics.
Utrecht has a dedicated course on speech sounds and their production and perception.
Utrecht studies word structure in depth.
Utrecht has a dedicated course on semantics and pragmatics. UCR examines dialogue and language in context through stylistics.
Utrecht connects theories of language acquisition and grammatical structure.
Utrecht studies language variation in social settings. UCR approaches related questions through sociology and communication.
Both use digital methods to work with data. UCR covers general data analysis, including text data.
Both develop empirical research and statistical analysis. UCR uses examples from psychology.
Utrecht studies sound systems through linguistic fieldwork. UCR offers broader qualitative research methods.
Utrecht’s capstone develops a proposal for the required thesis.
Utrecht requires a thesis. UCR’s optional research element sits outside the scheduled degree.
This is a coherent elective package, such as a minor or a second specialization.
Students choose these electives under Utrecht’s degree rules.
